answers.value: (a) Wire A has higher resistivity. (b) Wire B has greater drift velocity.
answers.scheme: (a) Slope of J-E is \(\frac{1}{\rho}\) (J = σE); A has the smaller slope, so higher resistivity. (b) \(I = neAv_d\), \(J = \frac{I}{A} = nev_d\), \(v_d \propto J\); for the same E, B has larger J, so greater \(v_d\). Or \(J = \frac{E}{\rho}\), \(v_d \propto \frac{1}{\rho}\), so B.
answers.note: The scheme itself adds, in italics, that since n_A and n_B differ for two materials it is difficult to find the variation of drift velocity.

answers.value: (i) Diagram of plane wavefront AB incident on the boundary and refracted wavefront \(A_1B_1\), with i and r marked. (ii) \(\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{c}{v} = n\), a constant (Snell's law).
answers.scheme: (i) Incident wavefront AB meeting the interface (μ1 above, μ2 below) at A; while B travels \(BB_1 = ct\) in the rarer medium, the secondary wavelet from A travels \(AA_1 = vt\) in the denser medium; refracted wavefront \(A_1B_1\); angles i and r marked. (ii) \(\sin i = \frac{BB_1}{AB_1}\), \(\sin r = \frac{AA_1}{AB_1}\), \(\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{ct}{vt} = \frac{c}{v} = n\) (constant). Any alternative method accepted.

answers.value: \(n = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}\) derived
answers.scheme: Labelled ray diagram through prism ABC (i, e, r1, r2, δm, normals N, N'). For any prism \(A = r_1 + r_2\) and \(A + \delta = i + e\). At minimum deviation \(i = e\), \(r_1 = r_2\), so \(i = \frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\), \(r = \frac{A}{2}\). By Snell's law \(\mu = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}\), giving \(\mu = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}\).

answers.value: (a) \(r_n = \frac{n^2h^2\epsilon_0}{\pi m e^2}\), so \(r \propto n^2\). (b)(1) In the Sun / stars. (2) Mass defect: the difference between the sum of the masses of a nucleus's protons and neutrons and the mass of the nucleus.
answers.scheme: (a) \(\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Ze^2}{r^2}\) ...(i); \(mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}\) ...(ii); squaring (ii) and dividing by (i): \(r = \frac{n^2h^2\epsilon_0}{\pi m Z e^2}\); for hydrogen Z = 1, \(r = \frac{n^2h^2\epsilon_0}{\pi m e^2}\); h, m, e, ε0, π constant, so \(r \propto n^2\). (b)(1) Sun / stars. (2) Difference between the mass of a nucleus and the sum of the masses of its protons and neutrons; or the mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of its nucleon masses; or difference between expected and real mass; or \(\Delta m = [Zm_H + (A-Z)m_n - m(_ZX^A)]\) (\(m_H\) or \(m_p\)).
